title: Know the strong, keep to the soft
hookLine: know the strong, keep to the soft, and be the valley of the world (Tao Te Ching 28)
carry: know strength, keep to the soft, be the valley
last: THE SAGE CASTS NO ONE AWAY.

lines: FROM THE TOP OF A RIDGE.
cards: From the top of a ridge, the whole landscape seems to be leaning one way. Streams run down. Paths wind down.

Birds drop down into the trees below. Down there, at the bottom, is the valley, and everything ends up in it: the water, the soil, the green, the people who built the village along the river. The peak gets the view.
The valley gets the life. Chapter twenty-eight of the Tao Te Ching asks a person to choose the valley on purpose, while knowing full well what it's like to stand on the peak.

teach.h: KNOW THE STRONG, KEEP THE SOFT.
teach.b: First, know the strong, keep to the soft. The chapter opens with a pair. In the Chinese, the words are male and female.
Know the male, it says, but keep to the female. Some readers hear in the pair the strong and the soft. The point is not to be ignorant of strength.
You know exactly what it is. You just don't live from there.

Second, the valley of the world. Do that, the chapter says, and you become the stream-bed of the world, the low channel everything runs into. Later it says the same with another word: the valley of the world.
Low, open, receiving. As with the ridge and the valley a moment ago, the high place is admired, but the low place is where things gather.

teach.h: BACK TO INFANT, BACK TO UNCARVED.
teach.b: Third, back to infant, back to uncarved. Then the chapter reaches back. It says that whoever is the stream-bed of the world returns to being an infant, and whoever is the valley returns to the uncarved block.

Those are two pictures you've already met: drifting like an infant, eight days ago, and the plain uncarved wood, nine days ago. Here the book ties them together. The soft way leads back to the beginning.

The chapter ends with the uncarved block split up into useful vessels, and the sage, put to use, becoming a leader of officials. And then a final line, which some translators render as: the great carver does not cut.
The best shaping, in this picture, leaves the thing whole.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching treat chapter twenty-eight as a way of carrying strength: knowing how to be forceful, and choosing receptiveness and humility instead.

o: pretending to be weak so others underestimate you
staying humble by never using any strength
knowing strength, but keeping low, soft and open

s: chapter twenty-eight says to stay ignorant of strength
it says know the strong, and keep to the soft. you know it; you just don't live from there.
the chapter ties the valley back to the infant and the uncarved block
the stream-bed of the world returns to the infant; the valley of the world returns to the uncarved block.
the chapter ends by praising the carver who cuts the most
its last line, as some translators render it: the great carver does not cut.

games.q: you know how to be strong, and you could win this one by pushing. you're reading chapter twenty-eight. what does it ask?
o: pretend you have no strength at all.
know the strong, and keep to the soft.
games.why: know the male, keep to the female, and be the valley of the world: low, open, the place everything runs to.

practice: Let your shoulders drop, the way water runs downhill.
Bring to mind one place where you could push, an argument, a deadline, a person who's slow, and picture the soft way instead: a lower voice, an open question, a moment of making room.
You're not giving up your strength; you're choosing not to lead with it.

wordCard.voice: Be the valley. Chapter twenty-eight's picture of a person who knows strength and keeps to softness, low and open, where everything gathers. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, wéi tiānxià xī: be the stream-valley of the world, from Tao Te Ching 28.

carryVoice: Your line: know strength, keep to the soft, be the valley. The peak gets the view; the valley gets the life. See you tomorrow.
